name: @attache/app
description: Attaché — an Envoy config workbench in the browser. Check a config, see what connects to what, and find out where a request actually goes. Run it with npx @attache/app.
author: Louis Emmett
//publishConfig: Scoped packages are RESTRICTED by default, and restricted publishing needs a paid npm plan — so without this the first release fails with a 402 that no dry run catches, because --dry-run never makes the access check. Set here rather than passed as --access public on the command line so that publishing by hand from a laptop cannot differ from publishing from CI.
//engines: A floor, not a support statement: the bin uses only node: specifiers, ?? and optional chaining. CI builds and tests on 24.

scripts.//og: Regenerates the link-preview image from public/og.svg. Deliberately NOT part of `build`: it needs rsvg-convert (brew install librsvg), which CI does not have and should not need — the PNG is committed, because a social preview that silently disappears when a toolchain is missing is worse than one checked into the repo.

//: No runtime dependencies, deliberately. What ships is a prebuilt dist/ with everything already bundled into it — React, @attache/core and its `yaml` — and a bin that serves it using nothing but Node built-ins. So `npx @attache/app` downloads one small package and runs, instead of resolving an install tree first. That is the whole point of the npx route: somebody with a production config full of private keys should be able to get a local tool up in one command, without it going anywhere near a website.
